b.t: Text

A desire to total up the results of the development of philosophical thought in the 20th century, to analyze the respects in which it has been distinctive, its successes and failures, has become clearly manifest in the bourgeois literature of the past two decades. There is nothing surprising in that fact as such. The mid-20th century is a chronological landmark of sufficient importance to impel thinkers to look behind them and give thought to the path they have traversed, while World War II and the cleavage of the world into two systems were trials of sufficient seriousness to compel a new look not only at the political but the intellectual history of the first half of this century. The fact that Marxism has become the most important factor in the entire ideological life of the contemporary world has destroyed the academic calm of bourgeois philosophy and compelled Western thinkers to undertake a review of their intellectual arsenal.

Another important factor has also contributed to the need to balance the books. The bourgeois literature is ever more clearly (and on an increasingly tragic note) recognizing the fact that the teachings and concepts that quite recently were grouped under the category of “classical 20th century philosophy” are in a state of crisis and do not identify the state of bourgeois philosophy in the 1950’s and 1960’s. The values on which that philosophy is oriented have changed, and along with them there has been a change in the subject matter, the language, and methods of philosophical thought.

The philosophical trends of the first half of the 20th century have come to the end of their development. This holds for neo-Kantianism, neo-Hegelianism, Bergsonism, pragmatism, and others. Processes of crisis are to be seen in theories that gained popularity comparatively recently (neopositivism, neo-Thomism, and existentialism). Having excited the world of philosophy only a short while ago, they have lost their novelty and, to a considerable degree, become subject matter for history texts. Theories and teachings that were born or took shape in the postwar period are striving to take the place of the old authorities. A fierce competitive struggle is under way between them for predominance in the philosophical marketplace and for the right to be termed “the characteristic philosophy of the 20th century.”

In a word, the accounting has proved, regardless of the subjective desires of the historians, to be an obituary for ‘classical 20th century philosophy.” The deflation of the “classical” writers has intensified the mood of crisis and given birth to a flow of critical literature, enlarging the scale of quests for “new contacts between philosophy and reality.”

It is no exaggeration to state that bourgeois philosophy is today in a process of reorganization, while the new look at its values is itself critical in nature. Something similar had previously occurred at the beginning of the century.

It is interesting that the principal problem over which lances were broken at that time has today again emerged into the forefront, and has taken on new life in all its scope. This is the question of what it is that is specific to philosophy: wherein its subject matter, tasks, functions, and approach are distinctive. Even the manner in which the question is posed has remained the same as a century ago. Bourgeois thinkers are seeking to define that which is specific to philosophy by examining its relationship to science, on the one hand, and to ideology on the other (the latter is regarded as a “value orientation,’ as the historically determined type of world view of a given society). This formulation of alternatives, involving the posing of science and ideology as two independent, mutually exclusive forms of intellectual activity, has never been seriously questioned in the past half-century. Debates have proceeded only over which of the two alternatives to give preference to in resolving the dispute over what is specific to philosophy.

Running ahead of ourselves for a moment, it may be stated that the bourgeois philosophers of the first half of the 20th century have been inclined to settle the choice between “science and ideology” in favor of the former; or, to be more exact, not so much in favor of science as “against ideology.” The opinion that took shape under the influence of the successes of natural science, to the effect that the progress of all knowledge is associated with liberating it from “values,” has underlain the programs of a number of trends that took shape in the twenties and thirties of the present century.

In that period, one of active attack upon the vestiges of feudalism in the social and intellectual spheres, a period of a tempestuous process of industrialization along with the first practical triumphs of the alliance of industry and the experimental sciences, popularity was enjoyed by the view of philosophy held by the Enlightenment, according to which the sterility of philosophy for practical purposes is the consequence of the violence done by age-old illusions and ideological prejudices. Philosophy needs only be freed from “external” importations, and its subject matter and method, its functions and tasks, need only be properly defined and it would endow mankind with successes no less significant than those of science.

Bourgeois philosophers of the second half of the 20th century are increasingly abandoning this viewpoint. The very notion that it is possible to free philosophy of ideological influences is being placed in doubt. Even though positivism continues to be the dominant type of philosophy (particularly in Britain and the United States), the ideal of a “rigorously scientific philosophy” no longer induces the former enthusiasm. Continuing their quests for that which is specific to philosophy in the most diverse directions, bourgeois thinkers are more inclined to orient thems e l v p upon ideology than upon science.

The idea that postwar Western philosophy has, to a considerable degree, taken shape as a negation of the “classical” philosophy of the first half of the 20th century will take on greater concreteness if we direct attention to certain important slogans, moods, and movements comprising the channel through which the shaping of philosophy occurred during the first half of the 20th century, and if we trace the ultimate destiny of these ideas.

As we know, the appearance and shaping of new schools took place in the course of criticism of 19th century philosophical thought and, above all, of classical German philosophy. This is why it is customary in the West to depict the 20th century as a “permanent revolution in philosophy” o r even as a “philosophy of revolution” (See Walter Kaufmann, Critique of Religion and Philosophy, New York, 1961, p. 20).

In fact, there has not been one bourgeois philosophy or current of any influence that has not claimed to have made a fundamental reorganization of philosophy in accordance with the new spirit of the times, new problems, new scientific data. Husserl and Dewey, the neorealists and critical realists, Nietzsche and Santayana, Whitehead and Bergson, Russell and Wittgenstein, N. Hartmann and the “philosophers of life” proclaimed their intention of destroying the structure of the old philosophy and of creating a fundamentally new concept of philosophy.

All regions and aspects of philosophy have been subjected to ”revolution”: the notions of its subject matter and method, its function and language, its relationship with science and experience. The “innovations” had the most diverse directions and acted in diverse forms.

Those who themselves participated in the new movements were inclined to describe them as meaningful trends in philosophy. To a certain degree this really was so. In the process of critical negation of earlier philosophy, a definite amount of constructive work was done. New fields for philosophical research were opened, new problems were posed while old ones were rendered more precise and reformulated. The methodology, logic, and language of philosophy were subjected to careful analysis. But nonetheless there was, as a rule, a poor awareness of the most important reason for the “reconstructions’’ that were everywhere under way the ideological one. In the social and intellectual climate of the first decades of the 20th century, the “revolution in philosophy” was an ideological reaction to the very style of thought produced by the dominance of ”monarchical” philosophical systems. By contrast to the former, “freedom of quest,” “a democracy of theories,” and “the equality of principles” were proclaimed (slogans whose specific social analogs it is not particularly difficult to find). The liberation of philosophy from the oppression of “absolute principles” meant, for many, liberation from the pressure of official, canonized, stagnant ideology. It is no accident that one of the components found throughout this movement was a criticism of traditionalism. For all the diversity of the “innovationist” schools, they had one characteristic in common: a negatively critical attitude (often going as far as nihilism) to previous philosophy.

The criticism of traditionalism was expressed in attempts to separate modern philosophy from the teachings and conceptions to which major attention had been given in academic courses in the history of philosophy, and above all from the rationalism of the 18th and 19th centuries. The history of philosophy was proclaimed a discipline having no relationship to the solution of contemporary problems, an assemblage of confusions and errors that were studied only in order that they not be repeated in the future.

Even when the philosophy of the past was not openly discarded, it was “read anew” in such a fashion that that portion of its content which bore on current disputes among new trends inevitably took the center of the stage.

Certainly the criticism of past philosophy included rational aspects, but the selection, from the history of prior thought, of diverse and often contradictory objects for criticism, and the discordant evaluations arrived at of various teachings, are evidence that the goal sought in bourgeois philosophy in the twenties and thirties from the very outset was not only that of a meaningful review of the history of philosophy, but that of ideologically negating it. The history of philosophy was employed as a means of ideological struggle, and criticism of the philosophy of the past was a means for affirming the new notion of the social function of philosophy.

Another effective means for overcoming the “ideological weed-bed” of philosophy was held to be its concretization, the transformation of philosophy from a speculative discipline to a special one, a particular branch of positive knowledge based on facts and experience. The movement for concretization and narrow specialization was outlined as early as the end of the 19th century and comprised one of the consequences of the revolution in natural science.

Against the background of stupendous discoveries in the experimental sciences and the effectiveness of experimental methods, the old techniques of philosophizing appeared anachronistic to many thinkers. Active measures were taken to seek out new spheres and forms of philosophical activity and to apply in philosophy techniques that had demonstrated their fruitfulness in the natural sciences.

This movement, again, proceeded under the flag of emancipation of philosophy from “ideological fetishes” (from undemonstrable speculations, the concept of philosophy as the “science of sciences,” from natural philosophy and historicism, etc.). The internal core of the meaning of this movement was, in Dewey’s expression, the quest for certainty or a “solid foundation” for philosophy. As an antidote to speculative flights of fancy and “ideological generalizations,” the goal was advanced of transforming philosophy into a “special discipline,” “a rigorous science,” “empirical research,” etc.

The movement to make of philosophy an empirical and specialized discipline took different forms in different countries, had a variety of shadings, and differed greatly in content. Here we see both a movement for a philosophy of concrete disciplines, a “philosophy of science,” “of culture,” “of art,” etc., and the movement of proponents of “practical philosophy,” who held that useless and sterile metaphysical abstractions must yield place to concrete investigations, as well as the so-called “empirical movement” demanding a reconstruction of the structure of philosophy on the solid foundation of “the facts of experiment.” Under the banner of the quest for certainty there also developed the broad school of “Lebensphilosophie” (this relationship is manifest with particular clarity in the work of Wilhelm Dilthey), which later took the form of existentialism.

Of course, it would be wrong to believe that the movement toward narrow specialization and concretization was all-embracing. Despite the furious criticism of speculation and “systembuilding,” speculative philosophies never disappeared from the arena of bourgeois philosophy.

Bergson and Croce, Santayana and Whitehead, Bosanquet and Hocking were certainly in demand among the Western intelligentsia. But in the work of these thinkers, too, the idea of ”systembuilding” was changed in accordance with the spirit of the times. Virtually all of them expressed criticism of ”metaphysics” and refrained from deductive derivation of systems from “absolute principles.” System-building was replaced by “systematics,” rationalist deduction by intuitive “discrimination of essence,” and so forth. However, despite the modernization of their arsenal, these trends were no longer able to lay claim to intellectual leadership. They were increasingly pressed by philosophical teachings developing under the banner of transformation of philosophy into a concrete discipline on a par with natural science.

Pretensions to the effectuation of a “revolution in philosophy,” and to its transformation into an experimental science containing only verifiable, empirically confirmable knowledge, are particularly characteristic of Anglo-American philosophy and, above all, of its neopositivist varieties. Neopositivism demanded that philosophy be freed from undemonstrable metaphysical postulates, and that it be cleansed of the factors of personal subjectivism and ideological values (for greater detail on this, see V. A. Lektorskii, “From Positivism to Neopositivism” [Ot pozitivizma do neopositivizmu], Voprosy filosofii, 1966, No. 9). The following were advanced as primary methodological principles: orientation in terms of the scientific mode of thought, rigorousness and precision of philosophical reasoning, verifiability of philosophical propositions, applicability to the philosophy of the apparatus of science, and, above all, that of mathematical logic.

As we know, this trend provided the impetus for a movement that went beyond the confines of neopositivism as such, and toward what was called the “metaphilosophical movement.” Its essence resolved to the fact that the traditional “external” concerns of philosophy - the world, man, and knowledge - are replaced by an investigation of various components of philosophy itself: its language, logic, methodology, mode of function in society, etc. Correspondingly, disciplines such as “meta-logic,” “meta-ethics,” “meta-epistemology,” etc., came into being.
A similar process was to be seen in sociology.

Despite the increasing chasm between philosophy and sociology, the latter also developed under the slogans: “Down with ideology! Long live empiricism! ” The task was posed of transforming the science of society into a “concrete,” “experimental,” “practical science” engaged not in normative prescription but in establishing certain truths about facts having real existence.

As a necessary preliminary condition for the transformation of sociology into a “social science,” the demand was made that it be freed from “social metaphysics,” the historical approach, and the influences of ethics and politics.

This reorganization had very serious significance to all of social knowledge. The movement for a concrete sociology, which developed under the banner of “de-ideologization,” very quickly led to the establishment of the dominance of empiricism. The trend to narrow problems, the predominance of quantitative analysis, an orientation toward questionnaires, interviews, and statistical investigation of purely phenomenal manifestations of sociil consciousness have become virtually canonical criteria for “serious sociology,” which is increasingly undergoing transformation into “social engineering.B Its “therapeutic” function - the curing of every conceivable sort of disease of society, the modification of social conflicts, the maintenance of stability in society, and so forth - are given pride of place.

A second important consequence of the reorganization of sociology was the decline of social philosophy. With the exception of a few figures such as Pareto, Weber, Toynbee, and Sorokin, whose work is commonly regarded as a tribute to the traditions of the 19th century, fewer and fewer supporters of that discipline are found among professional sociologists. At best, it is assigned the logic of social research, purification of the language of sociology, and similar “technical” tasks. In other words, social philosophy is conceived of as “meta-sociology.”
All the above changes in the realm of philosophy and sociology have had a most serious influence upon the content and organization of work within the contemporary philosophy of the West.

A contemptuous attitude toward the history of philosophy, narrow specialization, and the counterposing of philosophy to sociology have led to sharp differentiation among philosophical theories. Whereas 19th century philosophy was characterized by a relatively limited number of positions held and the presence of common ground of content among the various theories, what strikes the eye upon examination of the philosophy of the first half of the 20th century is the abundance of currents, groups, positions, techniques, and philosophical languages.

This differentiation has complicated relationships within bourgeois philosophy itself; it has led to the drawing of lines of demarcation among trends and groups, promoted the breakdown of communications among them, and deepened self-isolation. This “xenophobia” of schools and trends is manifested in the most diverse forms: the publication of journals designed for a narrow group of specialists, the organization of conferences and symposia to which representatives of other trends are not invited, the absence of a common language at international philosophical congresses, etc.
Differentiation is also occurring within schools.

For example, the entire history of neopositivism has been characterized by the splitting off of independent groups which gradually lost the community of subject matter they had had and isolated themselves in tight little circles. The same thing happened in existentialism, in which a number of variants of “Lebensphilosophie” are in serious conflict with one another. The erosion of national philosophies and the fragmentation of schools led to the establishment of new types of connections. Groups and trends come into being not on the basis of a common world view, but on the basis of similar solutions to special problems in philosophy: knowledge, values, etc.

Evaluating as an entity the so-called scientistic movement in the philosophy of the first half of the 20th century, one may say that the idea of orienting philosophy on science was, in itself, certainly fruitful. In the pursuit of this approach, it proved possible to overcome many unfounded pretensions and illusions of philosophy, to open new realms of philosophical investigation, to pose new problems and reformulate old ones, and so forth. However, in the light of the fact that the participants in this movement sought to subordinate philosophy to new dogmas and canons without regard to its own laws, specific purposes, and functions (i.e., guided themselves by very definite ideological motives), philosophy faced serious difficulties. A situation arose by the mid-20th century which bourgeois philosophers themselves regard as critical in the highest degree. Isolation from the history of philosophy, loss of communication among schools, indifference to traditions of national culture, pettiness of themes, formalism, distraction by the “philosophy of philosophy” at the expense of the philosophy of reality, loss of a taste for problems of world view, etc., have all reflected themselves fatefully upon the position of philosophy in society. Attempts to give philosophy a practical character, directing it to attainment of truths verifiable by experience, turned out in practice to be loss of contact with praxis, as this meant indifference to broad problems pertaining to world view that today concern millions of people.

“When a clergyman loses faith, he abandons his calling; when a philosopher does so, he redefines his subject.”
— Bertrand Russell [retranslated]

However, the past experience did not simply disappear without trace. It demonstrated the fictitiousness of philosophical revolutions, dispelled many illusions, revealed the groundlessness of many claims, and brought modifications of programmatic statements. It was also of definite significance in changing the direction of quests for the specific meaning of philosophy.

If, from this standpoint, we attempt to define the distinctive features of the crisis of bourgeois philosophy of our day, we are sharply struck by the unpopularity of the slogan of de-ideologization of philosophy and by the clear loss of authority of “scientific philosophy.”

As we will recall, in the first decades of the 20th century virtually all new schools advanced programs for a ‘fundamental reorganization of philosophy.” Today such declarations are a rather rare phenomenon, and the matter is not merely that few original theories are now to be found. The very idea of the need for a fundamental break with the past in philosophy has been bankrupted. Even ‘innovators” do not seek to advertise their departure from tradition. Despite increasing dissatisfaction ,with the existing state of things, and regrets with respect to the false steps taken in prior decades, sweepingly destructive criticism is unpopular.

The conservative movement aimed at restoring old forms of philosophy to their place has grown in scale and become stronger. The innovative programs of the newest variants of neopositivism and existentialism, and of the representatives of philosophical anthropology, have been compelled to wage, in the philosophical marketplace, a competitive struggle with the “traditionalist” programs of the neo-Thomists, neo-Orthodox, and neo-Aristotelians.

In both the theoretical and ideological respects, philosophical conservatism is a complex phenomenon displaying diverse and often contradictory tendencies. In the rehabilitation of ideas of the past, one can see reactionary attempts to adapt systems of the past to the ideological needs of the present day. Recourse to the past has as its purpose employment of the authority of the history of philosophy to sustain theories that have become decrepit and obsolete and to veil falsification of truly progressive rationalist ideas and traditions. At the same time one can identify certain progressive factors in the philosophical doctrines under examination: an attempt to restore to their former place the rational guesses of the earlier philosophy, to take a definite positive position with respect to continuity in the history of philosophy, contrasted to philosophical modernism and nihilism, attempts to find a way out of the crisis by restoration of forms of philosophizing that had justified themselves at various times in the past, and so forth.

The new view of tradition has compelled bourgeois historians to take a new view, as well, of the theoretical interdependence of the schools and trends now in conflict. Ideas of “synthesis” and of “unity in pluralism” have become very fashionable. Moods of dissatisfaction with the in-group isolation of philosophers and the practice of mutual hostility have become quite widespread. Voices are heard with increasing frequency with respect to the need to begin a dialogue between “cultures and schools in philosophy” so as to shed light upon points of contact and common problems and standpoints. Bourgeois philosophers appeal, from the podium of congresses and conferences, for a cessation of the policy of isolationism and for establishment of mutual understanding with the purpose of developing a common platform.

Nor is there a shortage of recipes for the attainment of unity. Some contend that philosophical differences and mutual negation are based upon purely semantic disagreements and that, therefore, the escape from the crisis has to be found in some semantic reform. Philosophers of the existentialist persuasion hold that the lack of communication among philosophers of the West arises as a consequence of the fact that methods specific to philosophy have not been developed and that there has been an uncritical transfer into philosophy of the modes of thought distinctive to science. Thomists are appealing, with new strength, for separatism and pluralism to be overcome through recourse to the history of philosophy. More active steps are being taken to overcome the barriers of dogma separating Thomism from other currents. Voices calling for “communication” and “mutual enrichment” and even for “a new reading of St. Thomas Aquinas” from the standpoint of phenomenology, existentialism, linguistic analysis, “dialectical philosophy,” and the like are resounding ever more loudly (see R. Harvanek, “The Crisis in Neo-Scholastic Philosophy,” Thought, Vol. 38, No. 151, 1963).

In this striving for unity, various meaningful motifs are being heard. Bourgeois philosophers admit that the present era has posed numerous new philosophical problems, the solution of which is impossible without joint action on the part of specialists of various disciplines. But separatism has as its consequence primitive methods of work, duplication of attacks upon problems already solved, and ignoring certain achievements of related trends. More and more philosophers are beginning to understand that their form of work has become an anachronism and obstacle on the path of development of philosophical knowledge.

A substantial factor impelling bourgeois philosophers to seek “unity in pluralism” is that the traditional individualistic activity of the bourgeois philosopher conflicts with the general nature of intellectual and ideological work in the era of imperialism. The process of standardization and unification that has affected all spheres of ideological life has necessarily extended to philosophy. State-organized capitalism in its monopoly stage requires organized feelings, an organized ideology, an organized mind. Whether bourgeois thinkers wish this or not, their activity is subordinated to this standard of intellectual life.

It is interesting to note that religion, which has always been marked by a sensitive response to social urgencies, has already responded to the demand for ideological integration by the ecumenical movement, which is today probably the most remarkable phenomenon in the religious life of capitalist countries. Something of an analogous nature is to be seen today in philosophy as well.

Nor must it be forgotten that a major factor compelling bourgeois philosophers to cross the barriers of their schools and seek a single platform is the existence of Marxism, which provides a monistic solution of a broad range of philosophical problems. The response to Marxism gives rise to disarray.and vacillations among bourgeois philosophers and at the same time pushes them to agreement in the struggle “against the common enemy.”

The dichotomy between system-building and narrowly specialized philosophies presently appears in a new relationship. The critique of “Grand Philosophie” that was characteristic of the first decades of the 20th century has been replaced by criticism of narrow specialization and attraction to specialized and “technical” problems of philosophy. Philosophies claiming to embrace a broad range of problems of world view are enjoying increasing popularity. One of the reasons for this change is the change in the nature and problems of scientific knowledge today. The development of science has posed acutely the question of the development of a new picture of the world, a new classification of sciences. The striving for synthesis that is characteristic of present-day scientific knowledge has given rise to a corresponding movement in philosophy.

The fact that the positivist trends are experiencing a degree of crisis is another important cause of this movement. In the twenties and thirties positivists advanced a number of valid demands and made a serious contribution to the treatment of problems in the philosophy of science, problems in the logic of methodology, and analysis of language. The demand for rigor and precision in philosophical reasoning, the verifiability of propositions in philosophy and, most important, an orientation toward a scientific type of thought seriously undermined the authority of frankly idealist and irrationalist currents. However, in their effort to fit philosophy into the Procrustean bed of elementary scientific methods and to place in question Its functions in the realm of world view (a development generally characteristic of scientism as an ideological movement) which developed in the course of the centuries and are of pressing interest today, the neopositivists have essentially undermined the ideal of a scientific philosophy which they themselves put forth. The past decade has revealed with particular clarity the untenability of neopositivist claims to have overcome “metaphysics,’ to have escaped the contradiction between materialism and idealism, and to apply the scientific method to philosophy. When the neopositivists moved from declarations to the implementation of their programs, it turned out that what underlay logical and linguistic analysis were the same “metaphysical” problems which they had claimed to have eliminated: problems of mind and matter, space and time, the nature of universals, etc. Even the analytical method, for which such great hopes were held, proved in many respects to be related to the methods employed by idealists in the past: Hegel, Leibniz, and others.

The process of transformation of the initial premises of positivism has now gone so far that the neopositivists themselves are no longer capable of identifying precise criteria by which one may distinguish “scientific” from “unscientific.” The conditions are thereby created for erasing the lines of demarcation between the scientistic type of philosophy and ”Lebensphilosophie,” religious philosophy, etc.

The tendency to dehumanize philosophy calls forth particularly marked condemnation from schools of the most diverse order. The effort of proponents of “rigorously verifiable knowledge” to transform philosophy into a discipline significant only for logic and cognition is being subjected to sharp criticism.

It is quite remarkable that the effort to find ultimate criteria for the exactness and certainty of knowledge in the realm of logic, methodology, and the theory of language has led many bourgeois philosophers, particularly young ones, to break with philosophy. Their contact with praxis is now in a sphere other than that of philosophy.
Most often, they become consultants at computer centers belonging to one or another corporation.

In the effort to detach the problem of the truthfulness of knowledge from problems of world view and axiology, the desire has been manifested, characteristic of a large part of the bourgeois intelligentsia, to separate itself from the struggle and confusions of the contemporary world and from sharp problems in the realm of world view. It is no accident that logical-linguistic analysis is often described in contemporary Western literature as philosophical “escapism” and “scientific asceticism.” Abandonment of efforts to resolve problems of vital importance in philosophy means, in fact, to recognize that these problems are irrational. It is significant that as the claims of positivism are revealed to be lacking in vindication, irrationalist and religious philosophies become revitalized.

The crisis of positivism is one of the important reasons why, today, the voices of bourgeois philosophers who place in the foreground the “metaphysical, ” moral, social, ideological and similar functions of philosophy have become so loud and so confident. It is striking that, as recently as the 1 9 4 0 ’ ~ ~ the idea that “metaphysical thought is passing through its final stage” (K.

Hamilton, The System and the Gospel, London, 1963, p. 1) seemed to be beyond question. Today many believe that metaphysics has taken a “new breath” (see Prospect for Metaphysics. Essays of Metaphysical Exploration, edited by Y. Ramsey, New York, 1961).

It is also characteristic that the revival of “metaphysics” is regarded by many as the most significant and determining characteristic of the philosophy of the future. Representatives of diverse trends are increasingly in agreement that the future philosophy has to be some sort of “higher synthesis.” The question of philosophy as a means of systematization, or even itself a system, is being raised once again. “From the time of the destruction of the great synthesis of Christianity and modern thought attained by Schleiermacher, Hegel, and the liberalism of the 19th century,” Tillich has written on this, ”a revulsion against systems has taken root in the minds of people who have not been willing to accept either alternative (the denial of faith o r of philosophy). They have too often been brought to confusion, and too many of the systems have suffered failure in order for them to undertake attempts to establish a new synthesis. But we have no other way out. And we must attempt to do this once wain” (Paul Tillich. Biblical Religion and the Search for Ultimate Reality, Chicago, 1956, p. 57).

Turning to concrete prognoses with respect to the future of philosophy (we examine them on the basis of the data of the American philosophical literature), they differ significantly and bear the imprint of the position currently taken by the respective authors. On the whole, it may be said that these differences are defined by discussions of the principal trends in contemporary bourgeois philosophy, and primarily by neopositivism, naturalism, existentialism, neoorthodoxy and neo-Thomism with respect to the interrelationships among philosophy, science, and ideology.

Popularity is enjoyed by the idea of synthesis of empirical and speculative philosophies. Many hold that the separation of empirical from speculative philosophies was a historically necessary phenomenon, albeit a temporary one, a sort of preparation for a future “synthesis,” and that today ”no task is more serious than unification of these two contrasting elements of 20th century philosophy” (M. White, The Age of Analysis, Boston, 1955, p. 242).

Emphasis is placed on the need for a world view that is effective and takes into consideration the diversity of intellectual and social experience. “We experience the need for a new, viable philosophy which, unlike the past, would react sensitively to the achievements of contemporary logic and science, metaphysics and theology, history and science, and would thus be in a position to keep more in step with the age in which we live” (P. Weiss, “The New Outlook,” in American Philosophers at Work, edited by Sidney Hook, N.Y., 1957, p. 306).
A “new vitality” has been gained by the notion in accordance with which the philosophy of the future has to be “synthetic” and “synoptic.”

Once again becoming “the queen of the sciences,” it must “direct its efforts to a far-reaching reorganization of the contemporary division of human knowledge” (R. Dewey, “The Future of Philosophy,” The Journal of Philosophy, Vol.

It must be stated, however, that the original positivist orientation toward science is objected to by members of the most diverse trends and schools. It is persistently emphasized that “metaphysics must develop its own procedures, applicable to its subject matter, rather than forcibly compelling the scientific method to work in a field reserved to it” (E. W. Hall, “Metaphysics,” in Twentieth Century Philosophy, edited by Dagobert Runes, 1947, N.Y., p. 170).

The overall motif of the criticism resolves to the fact that the history of contemporary philosophy allegedly testifies to the need. to differentiate between philosophical and scientific knowledge, and not to a need for collaboration between them.
Thus, the critique of positivism becomes a denial of the very idea of philosophy as a scientifically oriented discipline capable of rational proof.

This mood renders comprehensible the sympathy with which the position of religious philosophers is met in the West. According to the Thomists, the philosophy of the future will have to be “the teachings of St. Thomas Aquinas, which have not aged with the centuries,” which develop their own principles from within and do not need either “the positive assistance of science” or ideological defense (see G. P. Klubertanz, Introduction to the Philosophy of Being, New York, 1955, p. 278).

The “anthropological” viewpoint, in accordance with which the principal question of philosophy is “the problem of man,” his position in society and the characteristics of his behavior as a social being, and so forth, enjoys rather wide popularity (see F. Mayer and F. Brower, Patterns of a New Philosophy, Washington, 1955).

Increasing popularity is being acquired by the existentialist concept of philosophy, which centers attention upon “the existence of man,” “the living world of human experience,” with its anxiety, alarms, freedom, and creativity (D.
W ald) .

The question of conscious allowance for “value factors,” influences of a cultural, social, political and similar nature, is put with increasing frequency. Of considerable importance in this regard is the work done by bourgeois scholars in the study of the nature of values, intellectual culture, the mechanism of ideology, the social conditioning of knowledge, and the psychology of the creative process.

Along with the movement for a revival of the functions of philosophy with respect to world view, the rehabilitation of the standing of social philosophy that has occurred in the recent past attracts our attention. Ever more frequently, questions are posed and discussed that had previously been classified as “social metaphysics” (on the essence of the historical process, its motive forces, freedom and necessity in history, etc.). It is noteworthy that an increased interest in this discipline is observed not only among philosophers and sociologists, but among the representatives of other sciences. (1) The revived interest in social philosophy is due to a number of causes. Here one may direct attention to a need that has arisen in the course of accumulation of social knowledge - the need for a synthesized picture of social processes, the increasing significance of socio - ideological theories in the national and political movements of our day, to the effort of bourgeois theorists to counter historical materialism with some variant of a general theory of social development. In the writings of many sociologists, the notion of the need to revive social philosophy appears as the result of disillusionment with empirical sociology, which prove quite effective for the solution of partial problems but powerless in the face of the basic problems of society.

Investigators who at one time accepted with enthusiasm Weber’s idea of building a “value-free sociology” have been persuaded by their own experience that “a sociology free of values” is no more possible than a society free of values.

This conclusion is confirmed by the history of empirical sociology. The more than three decades of its development have persuaded many that “empiricism is not merely sociological methodology but social ideology” (Irving Louis Horowitz, “Introduction to the New Sociology,” in The New Sociology, I. L. Horowitz, ed., New York, 1964, p. 6), and, moreover, ideology of a very specific type - apologia for conformism and defense of the status quo.

It is significant that the theoreticians of “the end of ideology” who quite recently predicted “the extinction of ideological passions” under the conditions of “developed democracy” are today essentially abandoning the positions they held. Thus, for example, David Bell, who asserted as recently as the end of the 1950’s that, in contemporary highly organized “industrial” society, increasingly guided by social science and not ethical considerations, a “dying off of ideologies” is under way (David Bell, The End of Ideology: On the Exhaustion of Political Ideas in the Fifties, New York, 1961), is now compelled to record the activation of ideological struggle in the U.S. and the appearance of new ideological movements (particularly rightist ideologies) (David Bell, ed., The Radical Right, New York, 1964).

It is still early to speak of the character and distinguishing features of the bourgeois social philosophy of our day. At present, it is no more than desires and guesses with respect to its subject matter, method, functions, and goals that are being expressed. But even these things are of interest to us, inasmuch as they indicate to some degree the path of reorientation of contemporary social thought.

One is struck by the similarity of the wishes expressed with respect to social philosophy and philosophy per se. It is assumed that social philosophy must undertake the task of synthesis of social knowledge and simultaneously implement its coordination and integration. Particular emphasis is placed upon the need to revive the functions with respect to philosophical world view (an overall view of human history, social institutions, human relationships, etc.), the very functions that the “end of ideology” theorists regard as “an anachronism” not in accord with the level and character of knowledge of “developed democracy.” Contrary to the concept of the “anti-ideologists,” there is advanced the idea that “non-philosophical social science is no more possible than non-ideological social philosophy” (D. C. Hodges, “And the Withering Away of Social Philosophy,” Philosophy and Phenomenological Research, Vol. XXV, No. 4, 1965, p. 473).

It must be stated that assertions of this order are being made by sociologists of various camps, including liberally inclined critics disturbed by the dehumanization of modern social knowledge and its detachment from pressing social and intellectual problems. In their view, social philosophy is above all a theoretical foundation for some sort of humanist program capable of stimulating the masses to activity in the realm of culture and social change. This makes clear why the proponents of social philosophy are not satisfied by “general sociological” constructs of the type that Talcott Parsons, Sorokin, and other proponents of “Grand Sociology’’ have recently been active in erecting. Functionalism does not suit their purposes because of its conformism, justification of the status quo, and lack of prospects for the future. Considerably greater enthusiasm is induced by the teachings of C.

Wright Mills, which comprised an appeal for the founding of a humanist and at the same time critical social science. It is no accident that, after his death, his writings enjoy greater popularity and his teachings have gained more adherents than prior to the 1960’s.

Thus, the very logic of development of knowledge, culture, and the social experience of bourgeois thinkers has led to the conclusion that philosophy is by nature a matter of world view and, consequently, that it cannot be freed from the influence of ideology. Any attempt to transform philosophy into “pure science” by operations to eliminate “ideological overlays” will invariably fail because “the end of ideology” always turns out to be the end of what is unique to that discipline and its dissolution into other forms of knowledge. In other words, for philosophy to define itself through “ideological sterilization” results in its self-negation.

On the other hand, one hears more and more insistently the idea that the progress of philosophical knowledge and the attainment of verifiable truths are facilitated not by “revolutionary” reorganization of the subject, method, and functions of philosophy or efforts to find distinctive spheres of activity free of ideological overlays, but within the framework of ideology itself.

Ideology is a form that in one way or another places its imprint upon all human knowledge, which is thus limited within historical and social confines. But at the same time it is only in this form that the attainment of objective knowledge is possible.
All these admissions may be regarded to some degree as indirect confirmations of the positive value of the Marxist position that philosophy is by nature social, and is a matter of world view.

It is not uncommon for bourgeois thinkers to point directly to the primacy of Marxism in defining the nature of philosophical knowledge (consider simply the sociology of knowledge). It must be emphasized, however, that present-day Western thinkers are still far from seriously posing the question of the falseness of the very antithesis, “science or ideology.” Most often, the ideological conditioning of philosophical knowledge is understood as inevitably deforming it, as a “deviation” from the truth. The notion that ideology, reflecting progressive social tendencies, can serve as a powerful stimulus to the development of knowledge, is foreign to bourgeois thinkers.

In forming a judgment on the trend, evident in current Western thought, to reestablish the union of philosophy and ideology, it is also necessary to take into consideration that the motivations pushing various groups of Western scholars to hold high the functions of philosophy in terms of world view, morality, culture, and others, differ quite significantly.
The enthusiastic proponents of “value-oriented philosophies” include many humanistically inclined thinkers who are disturbed by the dangers contained in the anti-ideological movement.

They hold with justice that conscious abandonment of theoretical forms of world view, of the philosophical interpretation of urgent problems of morality, politics, and the like, opens the road to elemental prejudices and reactionary ideological myths, and transforms the masses into passive recipients of official propaganda.

As a rule, however, the positive constructs offered by philosophers of the secularist type clearly do not correspond to their “longing for metaphysics.” Often they stop half way, understanding that the vast difficulties on the way to creation of a rigorously demonstrable philosophical system involve the danger of sliding down to inferential speculations, to the introduction into philosophy of aprioristic principles, of intuitive and irrational methods, moral and political prejudices.

But among the advocates of philosophies having broad-ranging world views an even larger number consists of those for whom the praise of value disciplines and critique of positivism serve to discredit the very idea of scientific philosophy, to denigrate methods of rational proof in philosophy and, consequently, to establish the legitimacy of irrationalism and theism.

The raising aloft of functions of ideology and world view in this type of philosophy is often associated not only with an aggressively antiscientific attitude, but also with conscious support of the dominant ideology of contemporary capitalist society. Therefore this kind of restoration to honor of the world view functions of philosophy is to be regarded as a step backward when compared with the theories developed during the first half of the 20th century.
